title: How Charaka Read the Body
description: The Charaka Samhita -the text that compiled his teaching, isn't a list of remedies. It's a diagnostic framework. The premise underneath all of it is simple: the same substance can heal one person and harm another. The same food that settles a cold, dry body in winter might aggravate a hot, inflamed body in July. Context is the medicine.
content:
Around 600 BCE, a physician named Charaka was practicing medicine in Taxila, in what is now northwestern Pakistan. When a patient came to him, he didn't start with herbs. He started with questions. What's your digestion like? How's your sleep? What's the weather been like? What did you eat yesterday? His diagnostic method was systematic observation: body, environment, season, time of day. Only after he had a full picture did he prescribe anything.

The Charaka Samhita -the text that compiled his teaching, isn't a list of remedies. It's a diagnostic framework. The premise underneath all of it is simple: the same substance can heal one person and harm another. The same food that settles a cold, dry body in winter might aggravate a hot, inflamed body in July. Context is the medicine.

That premise is what Ayurveda actually is. Not a personality quiz. Not a list of foods to avoid. A framework for paying attention to context.

The doshas - vata, pitta, kapha are the language Charaka used for that context. Vata is movement: circulation, breath, nerve signals, the pace at which your gut processes food. Pitta is transformation: digestion, body temperature, the chemical work of breaking things down. Kapha is structure: lubrication, tissue building, immunity. You have all three operating at all times. The mix shifts based on season, age, stress, sleep, and what you've been eating.

When it's cold, dry, and you've been travelling or overworked, vata goes up. You feel scattered, your digestion slows, your sleep gets light. When you've been eating spicy food and working long hours in heat, pitta goes up. You feel irritable, overheated, your skin may react. When you've been sedentary and eating heavy food in winter, kapha goes up. You feel slow, congested, unmotivated. These aren't personality types. They're physiological states. They change. You adjust.

Three things Charaka prescribed that are still worth doing.

First: tongue scraping every morning before eating or drinking. Whatever coats your tongue overnight is partially processed material the body moved out of the system during digestion. Removing it before you introduce anything new clears the first stage of the digestive tract and gives you immediate feedback on what happened the night before. Thick white coating means kapha is high and digestion was slow. Thin yellow means pitta is active. This is data.

Second: eat your largest meal at midday. Charaka was specific about this. Agni “digestive fire” follows the arc of the sun. It peaks at noon and drops significantly by evening. The body is built to process food when it's warmest. A heavy dinner eaten at 9pm is asking a system running at 20% capacity to do 80% of the work. Shift your meal timing before you change anything else.

Third: stop being afraid of ghee. Charaka prescribed clarified butter in dozens of formulations. The short-chain fatty acids in ghee are gut-supportive, the fat-soluble vitamins it carries (A, D, E, K) are well-absorbed, and a teaspoon on rice or dal is not the cardiovascular event the 1990s told you it was. The research has shifted. Charaka was right.

What Ayurveda is not is a rigid set of rules. Charaka himself was clear that any principle had to be adapted to the individual in front of you. His clinical notes are preserved in the Samhita, they document cases where he departed from standard protocol because the patient's situation required it. The framework exists so you can be adaptive, not so you can follow a food list.

Start with tongue scraping for a week. Not because it will transform your health on its own, but because paying attention to what's in your mouth every morning is the beginning of actually noticing your body. That is the practice. Everything else is detail.
